text: Every tool you've built in isolation so far, array math, Kronecker products, unitary checks, Bloch-sphere coordinates, reproducible seeding, is about to become one small, real piece of software: a quantum math toolkit you design, build, and review yourself over the next four lessons.

The scope is deliberately small: one to two qubit systems, a fixed set of gates, X, H, and CNOT at minimum, probability computation, reproducible sampling, and one visualization. Noise simulation, circuit drawing, and optimized n-qubit tensor contractions are real, legitimate extensions, and all explicitly out of scope for this build. The toolkit follows a three-file layout, gates, simulate, and visualize, following Chapter 5's project-organization pattern. And this capstone isn't introducing new quantum concepts, it's forcing everything from Chapters 1 through 5 to work together in one piece of code that actually has to run correctly.

Lesson 23 builds gates dot p y and the core of simulate dot p y, state representation and gate application. Lesson 24 extends simulate dot p y with measurement simulation and builds visualize dot p y. Lesson 25 reviews the whole thing end to end against known results.

By the end of Lesson 24, starting from the all-zero state, applying Hadamard on qubit zero and then CNOT should give probabilities point five, zero, zero, point five, the Bell state: equal chance of ket-zero-zero or ket-one-one, never ket-zero-one or ket-one-zero. That's something you can verify by hand right now, and it's the benchmark the finished toolkit gets checked against in Lesson 25.
Next lesson is where the plan stops being a plan and starts being code: the gate matrices and the state-vector functions the rest of the capstone sits on top of.
